title: The Nuremberg Code

confidence.note: The trial record and the judgment containing the ten principles are fully documented. Who actually wrote the code (the judges, or the advising physicians Andrew Ivy and Leo Alexander) is debated, as is how much it owed to German research guidelines of 1931.

people: Andrew Ivy, American physiologist who advised the prosecution
Leo Alexander, American physician who drafted six principles in April 1947
Henry Beecher, Harvard anesthesiologist whose 1966 exposé revived the issue
summary: Judging Nazi doctors in 1947, American judges wrote ten rules for human experiments. The first was absolute: the subject's voluntary consent. Many researchers ignored it.
body: On 9 December 1946 the prosecution opened its case before an American military tribunal at Nuremberg against 23 German doctors and administrators. They were charged over the "euthanasia" killings of disabled people and over experiments on concentration-camp prisoners: freezing, high-altitude, malaria and sterilization experiments among them. In August 1947 the judges convicted 16. Karl Brandt and six others were sentenced to death and executed; seven defendants were acquitted.

Several defendants had argued that no international law or statement drew a line between legal and illegal human experimentation. Two American doctors working with the prosecution, Andrew Ivy and Leo Alexander, disagreed. On 17 April 1947 Alexander sent the prosecutors a memorandum of six principles, and the verdict expanded them into ten under the heading "Permissible Medical Experiments." The first became famous: "The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential." Others demand that risks be justified by the importance of the problem, that only qualified scientists do the work, and that subjects be free to stop.

The rules were less new than they looked. Germany had issued detailed research guidelines in 1931 that were still in force, and one critic argues that six of the ten principles derive from them. Nor did the code change much at first. Investigators tended to see it as "a good code for barbarians," not for themselves, and it had little impact in the United States. The US Public Health Service syphilis study in Alabama ran for another 25 years, and there is no evidence that it was ever discussed in light of the code.

Change came by other routes. The World Medical Association adopted the Declaration of Helsinki in 1964, building on the code and on its own 1954 statement of principles, and has revised it repeatedly since. In 1966 the anesthesiologist Henry Beecher published "Ethics and Clinical Research," describing 22 studies by respected investigators in prestigious journals that had put subjects at risk, often without consent. That article and the 1972 newspaper exposure of the syphilis study led to American legislation and, in 1974, a National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects, whose Belmont Report of 1979 still frames research ethics.

myth.tradition: After Nuremberg, the code became the rulebook that governed human experiments.
myth.record: For two decades many researchers, especially in the United States, treated it as aimed at Nazi crimes rather than their own work. Formal US regulation of human-subjects research came only in the 1970s, after Beecher's 1966 article and the exposure of the syphilis study in 1972.

links.note: The American study that ran on for decades after the code was written.

title: Streptomycin and the randomized trial

confidence.note: The trial's design and results are documented in the Medical Research Council's 1948 report and participants' recollections. Calling it the first randomized trial is contested, since chance allocation had been used before; who deserves credit for discovering streptomycin was settled in court but is still argued over.

place: Rutgers University, New Jersey; London and other British hospitals
people: Albert Schatz, Rutgers PhD student who isolated streptomycin
Selman Waksman, head of the Rutgers laboratory, Nobel laureate 1952
Austin Bradford Hill, medical statistician who designed the trial
Philip D'Arcy Hart (1900–2006), physician on the design team
Marc Daniels, physician appointed to coordinate the trial
John Crofton, Brompton Hospital registrar who coordinated that hospital's part of the trial
summary: A scarce American antibiotic, a Britain short of dollars and a statistician's sealed envelopes produced the model for how new treatments are tested.
body: By 1943 Albert Schatz, a PhD student in Selman Waksman's soil-microbiology laboratory at Rutgers, had isolated streptomycin from the soil bacterium *Streptomyces griseus*. In 1944 William Feldman and Corwin Hinshaw at the Mayo Clinic showed that it worked against the tuberculosis germ. Waksman alone received the 1952 Nobel Prize, "for his discovery of streptomycin, the first antibiotic effective against tuberculosis"; Schatz later sued and won legal recognition as co-discoverer.

In postwar Britain the drug was expensive and paid for in scarce dollars, and the government bought only a little for testing. The statistician Austin Bradford Hill argued that it would be unethical not to use that small supply to find out properly what it added to the standard treatment, bed rest. The Medical Research Council enrolled young adults with acute, progressive tuberculosis of both lungs. Patients were assigned by random numbers whose sequence was hidden in sealed envelopes, and the specialists reading the monthly X-rays did not know who had received the drug.

In the first six months, 4 of 55 patients given streptomycin died, against 15 of 52 on bed rest alone. The trial also revealed the drug's weakness: tuberculosis bacteria in many patients became resistant, often after the fourth month, and then deteriorated. That lesson pushed doctors toward combining drugs.

The trial is often called the first randomized controlled trial. It was not quite. In 1931 the American doctors Amberson, McMahon and Pinner divided 24 patients into two matched groups and tossed a single coin to decide which group got a gold treatment, sanocrysin; it caused harm and showed no benefit. The MRC's own 1944 trial of patulin for the common cold was a carefully controlled multicenter study. What set the streptomycin report apart was its explicit concealment of allocation, which prevented doctors from steering patients into one group, and the clarity with which it said so. Alternation, not random allocation, remained the usual method for years afterwards.

myth.tradition: The 1948 streptomycin study was the first randomized controlled trial.
myth.record: Chance allocation had been used before, as in a 1931 sanocrysin trial decided by a coin toss. The streptomycin trial's real landmark was its concealed random allocation and the clear reporting of it.

title: The World Health Organization

confidence.note: The constitution's adoption, ratification and entry into force are documented in WHO's own records; the earlier international health bodies are well described by historians.

summary: Born with the United Nations, WHO defined health as complete physical, mental and social well-being, and inherited a century of cholera diplomacy.
body: At the 1945 San Francisco conference that created the United Nations, Brazil and China proposed an international health organization. A conference in New York drafted its constitution, signed on 22 July 1946 by 51 UN members and 10 other nations. It came into force on 7 April 1948, when the 26th of the 61 signatories ratified it, a date now marked as World Health Day. The first World Health Assembly met in Geneva that June. The constitution's preamble set an ambitious bar: health is "a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity," and its highest attainable standard is a fundamental right.

WHO was the heir of a long line. International health diplomacy began with the first International Sanitary Conference, called in Paris in 1851 over cholera and attended by only twelve states. The Office International d'Hygiène Publique followed in 1907 and the League of Nations Health Organization after the First World War. WHO absorbed their work; the older Pan American organization survived alongside it as WHO's regional office for the Americas.

links.note: WHO's greatest campaign.
WHO's 1978 call for health for all.
Cholera drove the first international health conferences.

title: Britain's National Health Service

confidence.note: The founding date, the nationalization of the hospitals and the 1951 charges are documented in government records and standard histories.

people: Aneurin Bevan, Labour minister of health who created the service
William Beveridge, author of the 1942 report on social insurance
Nikolai Semashko (1874–1949), Soviet People's Commissar of Public Health, 1918–1930
summary: On 5 July 1948 Britain made doctors, hospitals, spectacles and dentures free to everyone. Within three years it was charging for some of them.
body: The National Health Service began on 5 July 1948, the "Appointed Day" for a package of reforms that effectively created the British welfare state. William Beveridge's 1942 report had proposed state funding for health care but not how a service should work. The Labour health minister, Aneurin Bevan, persuaded his government to nationalize the entire hospital system, so the new service inherited some 2,800 hospitals with more than 500,000 beds. Demand that had been held back for years poured in; older people rushed to get spectacles. Free care at the point of use did not survive intact: charges for dentures and spectacles began in May 1951, and Bevan resigned that year, partly over the charges.

Britain was not alone in seeking care for all. In Soviet Russia, Nikolai Semashko, People's Commissar of Public Health from 1918, built a system funded from the national budget and, in theory, free to patients. New Zealand's Social Security Act of 1938 promised free health services for everyone, but doctors' opposition meant it was never fully implemented, and family doctors kept charging fees.

links.note: The other model: compulsory health insurance.

title: The Framingham Heart Study

confidence.note: The study's founding, enrollment and publications are documented by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and in its own archives. Sources differ slightly on the youngest age enrolled (28 or 30).

people: Thomas Dawber, study director from 1950
William Kannel, later director, co-author of the 1961 'risk factors' paper
summary: A Massachusetts town volunteered for decades of check-ups, and gave medicine the idea of the 'risk factor'.
body: By the 1940s cardiovascular disease caused about one in two deaths in the United States, and most Americans accepted early death from heart disease as unavoidable. In 1948 researchers began recruiting 5,209 men and women, aged roughly 30 to 62, in Framingham, Massachusetts, and examined them again and again to see who fell ill. In the 1960s the study linked smoking, cholesterol and high blood pressure to heart disease, and Thomas Dawber and William Kannel's 1961 paper popularized the term "risk factor." The study survived a 1969 federal order to phase it out and now follows its participants' grandchildren.

links.note: Cholesterol as a risk factor set up the case for lowering it.
The same years established smoking's other great harm.

title: Lithium for mania

confidence.note: Cade's 1949 paper is on record. His guinea-pig reasoning was mistaken (the animals were possibly poisoned), and lithium had been tried for mania in the 19th century, so 'discovery' is a generous word.

place: Bundoora Repatriation Mental Hospital, near Melbourne, Australia
people: John Cade (1912–1980), Australian psychiatrist
Mogens Schou (1918–2005), Danish physician who tested lithium in a controlled trial
summary: A psychiatrist in a makeshift lab injected guinea pigs with patients' urine, drew the wrong conclusion, and found a drug that still works.
body: Working in a makeshift laboratory at a mental hospital near Melbourne, John Cade injected guinea pigs with urine from manic patients, then with lithium salts, which left the animals "extremely lethargic," possibly from poisoning. In September 1949 he reported dramatic improvement in ten manic patients. Lithium had been tried for mania as early as 1871, and within two years of Cade's paper a patient died of lithium poisoning. Acceptance was slow: the Dane Mogens Schou published a controlled trial in 1954, but the US approved lithium only in 1970, the 50th country to do so.

links.note: The other new psychiatric drug of the early 1950s.
Schou's 1954 trial also used chance allocation, in the years after the MRC trial.

title: Smoking causes lung cancer

confidence.note: The 1950 studies, the British Doctors Study and the 1964 Surgeon General's report are all published and dated. The causal link is no longer disputed by scientists; the industry's statements of doubt are on the record.

place: London, UK; St Louis and New York, USA
people: Richard Doll, British epidemiologist
Austin Bradford Hill, British medical statistician
Ernst Wynder, co-author of the 1950 American study
Evarts Graham, co-author of the 1950 American study
Müller, author of a 1939 German case-control study
Luther Terry, US Surgeon General in 1964
summary: In 1950 two teams on two continents showed that lung-cancer patients were almost all smokers. Proving it, and getting people to act, took decades.
body: Lung cancer was becoming steadily more common among men. In 1950 two large studies appeared almost together. In the United States, Ernst Wynder and Evarts Graham compared the smoking histories of 605 lung-cancer patients with those of other patients; in Britain, Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill did the same in a study later enlarged to 1,465 cases. Smoking was far more common among the cancer patients. To answer the obvious objection, that sick people might misremember their habits, Doll and Hill showed that men wrongly suspected of lung cancer reported smoking much like the controls.

They were not the first. A German doctor named Müller published a comparison of 86 lung-cancer patients and 86 controls in 1939, and Schairer and Schöniger another in 1943. These were noticed in Germany but little cited elsewhere.

Case-control studies could be dismissed as coincidence, so Doll and Hill began a prospective study in 1951, recording the habits of 34,439 male British doctors and following their deaths for fifty years. Men born between 1900 and 1930 who kept smoking cigarettes died on average about ten years earlier than lifelong non-smokers.

Resistance was fierce. The eminent statisticians R. A. Fisher and Joseph Berkson rejected the causal claim. In 1954 American tobacco companies publicly declared that they did not believe their products were harmful, and filter cigarettes were rushed out to reassure smokers. The Royal College of Physicians of London issued a strong report in 1962. In the United States, a committee convened by Surgeon General Luther Terry reviewed more than 7,000 articles, and he released its report on Saturday 11 January 1964, a day chosen to limit the effect on the stock market. About 42 percent of American adults smoked in 1965; fewer than 20 percent did by 2011.

myth.tradition: Doll and Hill discovered in 1950 that smoking causes lung cancer.
myth.record: German researchers had published case-control evidence in 1939 and 1943, and an American study appeared the same year as Doll and Hill's. Their British doctors study, with a parallel American cohort study by Hammond and Horn reported in 1954, turned an association into compelling evidence.

links.note: Bradford Hill's previous landmark study.
Long-term follow-up linked smoking to heart disease too.

title: HeLa: Henrietta Lacks's immortal cells

confidence.note: The taking of her cells in 1951, their use in polio vaccine testing and the later agreements with her family are well documented.

people: Henrietta Lacks (died 1951, aged 31), the patient whose tumor cells became HeLa
George Otto Gey, Johns Hopkins cell biologist who grew the cells
summary: A sample of a Black patient's tumor, used without her knowledge, gave medicine the first immortal human cell line, and a lasting question about consent.
body: In 1951 Henrietta Lacks, an African American woman, was treated for cervical cancer at Johns Hopkins, where a biopsy sample was passed to George Gey's laboratory without her knowledge or consent. There her cells kept dividing indefinitely: HeLa, described as the first immortal human cell line, which Gey gave away free. She died on 4 October 1951, aged 31. Mass-produced at the Tuskegee Institute, HeLa cells helped evaluate the 1954 Salk polio vaccine trial. In 2013 the National Institutes of Health agreed with her family on access to HeLa genome data, and in 2023 her descendants settled a lawsuit against Thermo Fisher Scientific.
